title: The clause: complements
description: Learn how verbs select subjects, objects, predicative complements and prepositional dependents, and how those choices shape the clause.
example: The committee gave the designer an award for the new bridge.

intro: *The committee gave the designer an award for the new bridge* looks like a verb followed by a queue of phrases. The grammar sees something more precise: a subject outside the verb phrase, two internal objects, and a prepositional complement explaining what the award was for. The verb selects that arrangement, and the arrangement is what this chapter describes.

The chapter begins with the architecture of the clause: the major functions, the split between core and non-core complements, and the five canonical patterns. From there it turns to meaning, taking up semantic roles, the subject’s cluster of properties, objects and predicative complements. The final sections widen the view to prepositional verbs, particles, idioms, light verbs and verbs that live in several complementation patterns at once.

Two questions are worth asking together: what function does this expression perform, and what role does its referent play in the situation? The answers are related but not identical. Keeping them apart lets a description handle a passive, a ditransitive alternation or a prepositional verb without collapsing syntax into meaning.

blocks.text: *He always reads the paper before breakfast* contains three kinds of dependent, and only one of them fills a slot the verb demands. *Reads* is the predicator, the verb phrase that heads the clause. *The paper* is a complement, licensed by the verb. *Always* and *before breakfast* are adjuncts, adding information without completing the verb’s requirements.

The subject belongs with the complements but sits apart from them. It is external to the verb phrase, while objects and predicative complements are internal, which is why a canonical clause divides first into subject and predicate. The subject also carries a cluster of distinctive properties: position, case, agreement, inversion, tag formation and coordination behaviour.

*He looked at the paper*, *He seemed quite competent* and *He said that she was right* show complements in three forms: PP, adjective phrase and clause. Not every complement is an NP. Ask instead whether the verb licenses the dependent, and how that dependent fits the verb’s meaning.

blocks.text: *Kim gave Pat the key* and *Kim gave the key to Pat* describe one transfer with two different structures. In the first, *Pat* and *the key* are core complements, directly related to the verb and prototypically NPs. In the second, *to Pat* is still a complement of *give*, but it is non-core, realised by a PP, and *Pat* inside it is an oblique: an NP related to the verb only through the preposition.

The preposition contributes to the oblique’s semantic role; in *to Pat*, *to* marks the recipient. That does not make *Pat* an indirect object, because the syntactic relation differs: the NP sits inside a PP complement rather than acting as a direct complement of the verb. The two sentences are related in meaning, not in structure.

*Read* is intransitive in *She read*, transitive in *She read the letter*: same lexeme, different valency. Valency counts the syntactic complements a verb takes in a given use, not the semantic participants. A verb can be bivalent with a subject and object, or monovalent with a subject alone.

blocks.text: *She smiled*, *He washed the car* and *They gave me the key* are intransitive, monotransitive and ditransitive. The five patterns are shapes, not definitions of verbs. Add a predicative complement and the clause becomes complex: *This seems a good idea* is complex-intransitive, *I consider this a good idea* complex-transitive.

The labels describe clauses and verb uses, not lexemes in isolation. A verb can appear in more than one pattern, so the construction decides the label. Take *read*. *She read for a while* is intransitive; add *the letter* and it becomes monotransitive; add *us a story* and it is ditransitive.

A predicative complement makes the clause complex because it adds a second predication inside the same clause. *This seems a good idea* predicates *a good idea* of the subject; *I consider this a good idea* predicates it of the object. The relation is the same; the predicand has moved.

blocks.text: *Kim heard an explosion* and *The noise frightened Kim* place Kim on opposite sides of the same event: perceiver in one, affected party in the other. Roles track those differences. An agent is a prototypical conscious causer; a patient is affected by an action; an instrument is used by an agent; an experiencer feels or perceives; a stimulus arouses the feeling or perception. Theme is a broad role for entities involved without being agents or patients, and goal, source and recipient describe endpoints, starting points and receivers.

*Kim heard an explosion* has an experiencer subject; *They like me* has a stimulus object. Roles are not fixed by grammatical function. A single argument can carry more than one role: in *Kim bought the car from Pat*, Kim is both agent and goal, while Pat is both agent and source.

*Kim shot Pat* and *Pat was shot by Kim* describe the same situation with the same roles but present it from different perspectives. Presentational status is a separate dimension. In symmetric pairs such as *Kim married Pat* and *Pat married Kim*, the roles stay the same and the difference is entirely one of perspective. Passive does this, but it is not the only construction that can.

blocks.text: *The minister knows the candidates* shows the subject’s position and agreement in one stroke: the NP comes before the predicator, and *knows* agrees with it. Other properties cluster around those. The subject controls the pronoun in a tag (*The candidates know, don’t they?*), takes nominative case where a pronoun shows it, moves after the auxiliary in closed interrogatives, and plays a distinctive part in open interrogatives.

*The parcel was opened by Kim* has *the parcel* as subject although it is the patient, not the agent. Those properties identify the subject even when the clause is non-canonical. *There is one nurse here* has dummy *there* as subject and *one nurse* as displaced subject. *More important are the moral objections* has *the moral objections* as postposed subject.

*This one I’m giving to Jill* has *this one* as topic and *I* as subject. Subject and topic are different jobs. Passive, existential, extraposition and preposing constructions let a speaker choose which element is presented as subject and which as topic.

blocks.text: *Kim gave Pat the key* contains two internal complements, and only one of them is the thing given. *Pat* is the indirect object, characteristically the recipient; *the key* is the direct object, the patient or affected entity. Put the recipient inside a PP, as in *Kim gave the key to Pat*, and *to Pat* becomes a PP complement rather than an indirect object.

*I used a knife* requires its object; *He lent his car* allows it to be left out. Most objects are NPs, but their obligatoriness varies with the verb. A related passive gives a useful test: if an NP complement can become the subject of a passive, it is an object. The test is sufficient, not necessary, because some objects resist passivisation.

*Pat was given the key* and *The key was given to Pat* show that either object of a ditransitive can become the passive subject. The indirect object is usually the more expendable of the two. Languages with a distinct dative case do not necessarily allow that freedom.

*We thought it necessary to postpone the meeting* has *it* as object and *to postpone the meeting* as extraposed object. Objects can be extraposed. The clause behaves semantically like an object without occupying the object position syntactically.

blocks.text: *Kim seemed uneasy* and *He found Kim intolerant* both say something about Kim, but the predicand sits in a different place. A predicative complement expresses a property predicated of another element, its predicand. In the first sentence the predicand is the subject; in the second it is the object. The predicand is not the subject of the complement; it is the element the complement applies to.

Three tests separate a predicative complement from an object. Form is the first: a PC can be an AdjP (*nice*) or a bare role NP (*treasurer*), while an object is normally an NP. The passive is the second: *A minister was become by Ed* is impossible, so the PC does not become a passive subject. Case is the third: formal style allows *It was he who wrote it*, with a nominative pronoun.

Depictive and resultative readings describe different moments. *Kim seemed uneasy* characterises the predicand while the situation holds; *He found Kim intolerant* does the same for the object. Those are depictive readings. *Kim became angry* and *He made Kim happy* describe the state reached when a process ends: resultatives, which typically need a verb of change to supply the endpoint.

Obligatory and optional complements differ in how tightly they integrate. Take *He looked young*: the sense of *look* requires the complement. *He died young* is different; *young* is a predicative adjunct rather than a complement. Same form, different degree of attachment.

blocks.text: *Ed was quite competent* is the plainest copular clause: *be* relates a predicative complement to the subject, and the complement says what Ed was like. The construction covers several relations. Sometimes *be* does little beyond carrying tense; sometimes it identifies a value.

Two uses of *be* pull in different directions. Ascriptive *be* applies a property: *This is a good idea*, *Ed is competent*. Specifying *be* identifies a value: *The only problem is the cost*. Reverse a specifying clause and the relation survives, *The cost is the only problem*; reverse an ascriptive one and it does not.

Copular clauses form a family, not a single pattern. *Seem*, *become*, *remain*, *look* and *feel* take predicative complements with different degrees of obligatoriness and different semantic effects. *Become* is resultative, *remain* continuative, *seem* evidential. Calling them all copular does not make them interchangeable with *be*.

blocks.text: *Refer* insists on *to*: *refer to her article*. *Blame* selects *on* in *blame the accident on me*. In both, the preposition belongs to the verb’s lexical requirements rather than marking place or time freely. That is what separates *refer to* from *fly to Boston*, where *to* is an ordinary goal preposition.

Mobile and fixed prepositions behave differently under movement. A mobile one fronts with its complement and coordinates like any ordinary preposition: *the article to which I referred*, *I referred to her article and to several others*. A fixed one stays put: *the letters across which I came* is impossible, and only *the letters which I came across* works.

The distinction reaches adjunct placement and passives. A mobile preposition allows an adjunct between verb and PP: *I referred repeatedly to her article*. A fixed preposition generally does not: *I came eventually across these letters*. Prepositional passives are possible with some combinations and not others, depending on how tightly verb and preposition have fused.

blocks.text: *She put in her application* and *He brought the chairs in* show the same particle in two positions. A particle is an intransitive preposition that can sit between a verb and its direct object. Pronouns are stricter about order: *She put it in* is grammatical, *She put in it* is not.

A particle and a PP complement can look alike on the surface. Take *She jumped off the wall*: *off the wall* is a single PP complement. *She took off the label* is different: *off* is a particle and *the label* is the object. Look at the syntax, not only at the meaning.

*Give up the struggle*, *take me to task*, *pull my leg* are lexical units larger than a word, and their meanings cannot be built from their parts. Idioms need not form syntactic constituents. In *take me to task*, *to task* belongs to the idiom but the object separates it from *take*. The syntax still has ordinary constituents; the idiom lives above them.

blocks.text: *She gave him a kiss* says much the same as *She kissed him*, but the work is distributed differently. A light verb contributes relatively little meaning of its own; the noun complement carries the content. *We took a rest* corresponds to *We rested*, and *I made a calculation* to *I calculated*. The noun supplies the predicative content, the light verb the grammatical structure.

Light verbs earn their place by what they let the noun do. Modifiers and determiners attach to it: *She gave him an unusually passionate kiss*, *We took a well-earned rest*. Aspect and quantification can shift too: *He had a drink of my milk* suggests he drank only part of it, while *He drank my milk* suggests he drank it all.

*I had a bath* wobbles between two readings: that I bathed, or that I owned a bath. *He gave me a lick* can describe a dog licking me or a person allowing me a lick of ice cream. With light verbs the ordinary use of the same verb is always nearby, and context together with the noun’s interpretation decides which reading survives.

blocks.text: Most verbs occur in more than one complementation pattern, and *make* moves through several. *They made some cakes* takes a direct object; *They made me a filing cabinet* takes an indirect and a direct object; *They made me impatient* takes an object plus a predicative complement. The meaning stays recognisable while the syntax changes.

Four kinds of transitive/intransitive contrast are worth separating. The intransitive subject may match the transitive subject, as in *They shot him* and *They shot at him*. It may match the object, as in *The sun radiates heat* and *Heat radiates from the sun*. The transitive may simply add an object, as in *She drank some water* and *She drank*. Or the object may become the intransitive subject, as in *He broke the vase* and *The vase broke*.

Ditransitive/monotransitive pairs have their own logic. *I gave her the key* alternates with *I gave the key to her*; *They offered us $100* alternates with *They offered $100*. In *They fined us $100* and *They fined us*, the indirect object alone corresponds to the single object of the monotransitive.

Core/non-core contrasts and combined complements complete the picture. *He supplies arms to the rebels* alternates with *He supplies the rebels with arms*. *She kissed him on the cheek* has two complements, while *She kissed his cheek* folds their content into one. Complementation is a system of related options, not a fixed frame attached to each verb.

blocks.text: Complementation shapes what a verb can mean in a sentence. *They gave the key to Pat* and *They gave Pat the key* describe the same transfer, but the second presents Pat as an indirect object and the first puts Pat inside a PP. *They shot him* says he was hit; *They shot at him* does not.

A writer needs the pattern as much as the analyst does. A dictionary entry records the structures a verb permits, not just its meaning. *Refer* requires *to*; *blame* allows *on* or *for*; *supply* permits either *supply arms to the rebels* or *supply the rebels with arms*. You learn the pattern along with the verb.

Ambiguity often turns on complement structure. *Flying planes can be dangerous* can involve planes that fly or the activity of flying them, because one form can realise different functions. *The chicken is ready to eat* can describe the chicken as food or as an eater. Syntax narrows interpretation without always settling it.

blocks.text: Everything in the chapter radiates from the verb. It selects complements, and that selection decides whether the clause is intransitive, monotransitive, ditransitive, complex-intransitive or complex-transitive. The subject sits outside the verb phrase; objects and predicative complements sit inside. Core complements attach directly, non-core complements through a preposition.

Grammatical function and semantic role answer different questions. A subject may be agent, experiencer or patient; an object may be patient, stimulus or theme. Presentational status accounts for the way active, passive, existential and preposing constructions align the same roles differently. The subject is identified by grammatical behaviour, not by meaning.

Objects, predicative complements and obliques each have their own syntax. Prepositional verbs demand specified prepositions; particles sit between verb and object; light verbs lodge the main content in a noun; most verbs appear in several complementation patterns. To read a clause is to identify those choices and watch them shape the meaning.

blocks.title: A complement checklist
blocks.text: Find the verb and its subject. Identify the internal complements. Decide whether each is an object, a predicative complement or a PP complement. Check for a particle or an oblique. Then ask what semantic roles the participants have and whether a different construction would present the same situation differently.

worked: Take *The committee gave the designer an award for the new bridge*. The subject is *the committee*, the predicator is *gave*, and the two internal core complements are *the designer* and *an award*. *The designer* is the indirect object and *an award* is the direct object. *For the new bridge* is a PP complement expressing the reason or basis for the award.

The same situation can be presented as *The committee gave an award to the designer for the new bridge*. Now *an award* is the direct object and *to the designer* is a PP complement, with *the designer* as an oblique. The participants and their roles have not changed, but the syntactic functions have. That contrast is the core of this chapter.
application: When you analyse a clause, find the verb first. Its subclass tells you which complements to expect. Then identify the subject, objects, predicative complements and any PP complements. Do not assume that every phrase after the verb is an object: *at the paper*, *to Pat* and *in the box* are PP complements, while *the paper*, *Pat* and *the box* can be objects in other patterns.

Next, separate function from role. The subject of a passive is often the patient, not the agent. The object of *hear* is a stimulus, not a patient. A predicative complement ascribes a property rather than naming a participant. Keeping these levels distinct prevents a description from turning into a list of traditional definitions.

Finally, compare alternations. *Give the key to Pat* and *give Pat the key*, *shoot him* and *shoot at him*, *break the vase* and *the vase broke* are related patterns with different syntax and sometimes different meaning. The comparison shows what the verb licenses and what the construction adds.
reveal: In *The committee gave the designer an award for the new bridge*, the clause is ditransitive: *the committee* is subject, *the designer* is indirect object, *an award* is direct object, and *for the new bridge* is a PP complement. The related *gave an award to the designer* is monotransitive with a PP complement, and *the designer* is an oblique inside that PP.
recap: Clauses contain a predicator, complements and adjuncts. The subject is the external core complement; objects and predicative complements are internal. Core complements are directly related to the verb, while non-core complements are realised by PPs and contain obliques.

Semantic roles describe participants, while grammatical functions describe syntactic structure. The subject has a cluster of distinctive properties. Objects and predicative complements differ in form, meaning and behaviour. Prepositional verbs, particles, idioms, light verbs and multiple complementation patterns extend the basic system.

self_check.question: Name the five canonical clause patterns.
self_check.answer: Intransitive, monotransitive, ditransitive, complex-intransitive and complex-transitive.

self_check.question: What is the difference between a core complement and an oblique?
self_check.answer: A core complement is directly related to the verb and is prototypically an NP. An oblique is an NP related to the verb through a preposition inside a PP complement.

self_check.question: Give two tests that help identify the subject.
self_check.answer: Subject-auxiliary inversion in a closed interrogative, and the pronoun used in a tag.

self_check.question: How does a predicative complement differ from an object?
self_check.answer: A predicative complement ascribes a property to a predicand and can be an AdjP or bare role NP; an object normally names a participant and is an NP.

self_check.question: What is a light verb?
self_check.answer: A verb such as give, take or make whose main semantic content is supplied by its noun complement, as in give a kiss or take a rest.

options.feedback: An object is internal to the VP.
A preposed object can also precede the verb.

opening.prompt: In Kim gave the key to Pat, what is to Pat?

options.text: A PP complement containing an oblique
options.feedback: Pat is the complement of to, and the PP is the complement of give.
The indirect object construction is Kim gave Pat the key.
It does not ascribe a property.

options.text: I consider this a good idea.
options.feedback: This is the object and a good idea is its predicative complement.
That is complex-intransitive: no object.
That is ditransitive.

opening.prompt: What role does Kim have in Kim heard an explosion?

options.feedback: Kim perceives the sound.
Kim is not performing a deliberate action.
The explosion is the stimulus.

opening.prompt: Which form can be a predicative complement but not an object?

options.feedback: Predicative complements can be AdjPs; objects are normally NPs.
Both objects and PCs can be NPs.
PPs can be complements, but the contrast here concerns AdjPs.

closing.prompt: What is the subject of The parcel was opened by Kim?

options.feedback: It is the subject of the passive clause, though it has the patient role.
Kim is the agent in the by phrase.
The by phrase is a complement.

closing.prompt: Why is to me not an indirect object in They gave the key to me?

options.text: It is a PP complement, while objects are normally NPs.
options.feedback: The indirect object construction is They gave me the key.
The direct object is the key.
It does not ascribe a property.

closing.prompt: Which clause has an object-oriented predicative complement?

options.feedback: Intolerant is predicated of the object Kim.
Uneasy is predicated of the subject Kim.
Angry is subject-oriented.

options.text: An intransitive preposition between a verb and its object
options.feedback: In She put in her application, in is a particle.

options.text: A preposition with an NP complement
options.feedback: That is a transitive preposition or PP complement.
A light verb is a verb such as give or take.

closing.prompt: Which pair shows an object becoming the subject of an intransitive?

options.text: He broke the vase / The vase broke.
options.feedback: The transitive object corresponds to the intransitive subject.

options.text: They shot him / They shot at him.
options.feedback: The subject stays the same; the object becomes a PP complement.

options.text: I gave her the key / I gave the key to her.
options.feedback: This is a ditransitive alternation, not a causative/inchoative pair.

predict.prompt: Which pattern is They gave me the key?

options.feedback: Me is the indirect object and the key is the direct object.
The second complement is an object, not a predicative complement.
There are two internal objects.

guided.prompt: In He supplied the rebels with arms, what is with arms?

options.feedback: It is a non-core complement of supplied.
The related construction is He supplied arms to the rebels.
It does not ascribe a property.

transfer.prompt: In The parcel was opened by Kim, what role does the subject have?

options.feedback: The passive promotes the affected entity to subject.
Kim is the agent in the by phrase.
No experience is involved.

exit.prompt: Which expression is a light verb construction?

options.feedback: Give contributes little; kiss carries the main meaning.
That is the associated verb construction.
Give has its ordinary transfer meaning.
